name: Karl Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead a repair crew for an electricity company. My two-year technical diploma helps with the network diagram, but the real job is building or repairing the power line in front of us, safely and without sending a truck back for a missed part. I am proud when the younger hands learn to check the isolation twice. My partner and I have grown children, and we have begun looking at retirement figures without choosing a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little faster depot work is fine, but it does not replace the crew at a broken span. I use AI now and then to tidy a parts note, then measure the part myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Typical pay and several months saved give us a workable cushion while shifts stay steady. I want a retirement estimate before making a promise about leaving, and this mild AI change does not hurry the decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the repair rota and compare every drafted parts note with my site measurements. During the first year I would request a retirement income estimate and sit with my partner to compare it with our actual costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work, with ordinary care about later income. A tidy AI parts note cannot put the right mounting holes in a power line crossarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reject a tidy parts note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A crossarm might be the right length on a drawing but have the wrong mounting holes. I would check the physical holes before sending a truck for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the retirement estimate is disappointing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the ordinary shifts and review the date later. We have some savings, but a few months of expenses do not fund years away from work.

say: I would **welcome** shorter depot notes while keeping physical repair checks.
A **crew** still measures each bracket before ordering.
think: **Typical** pay and several months of savings make current shifts feel secure.
**Retirement** timing remains open until household costs and income estimates are compared.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and compare drafted parts notes with site measurements.
**Request** retirement estimate and compare it with household costs.
feel: **Calm** about present work, cautious about future income.
S0.quote: A tidy AI parts note cannot put the right mounting holes in a power line crossarm.
fieldNote: His **occasional** AI use stays in paperwork while field measurements govern orders.
He **seeks** retirement information without claiming a new exit date or guaranteed payment.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and verify drafted parts notes against measurements
Request retirement estimate before making exit decision

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that AI booking and buying could save trips if a crew can correct a bad order. I would ask for a trial on ordinary repair jobs before any new time target is set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on work lasts longer than desk ordering, but faster schedules could reduce paid callout hours. We have a few months saved, yet losing that income now would make the retirement figures worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new AI ordering screen on paid time and test it against six completed work sheets. In the first year I would send the wrong part numbers to the store manager and record whether the next order is corrected, while keeping the crew’s site checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible hours loss, though I can test the tool. A corrected order is useful; a rushed line repair is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mismatch would you send to the store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would send the pole type, the part the screen chose and the bracket we actually fitted. The store manager can then see where the rule failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept the new time target if orders improve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after we check actual travel, isolation and repair times. A faster AI bracket order does not shorten the isolation check beside a live power line.

say: I would **test** AI ordering before accepting new repair time targets.
**Field** crews should be able to correct wrong parts.
think: **Desk** ordering changes first, while physical line repair still needs crews.
**Possible** callout cuts could weaken my retirement income despite several months saved.
do: **Learn** AI ordering screen on paid time using six completed work sheets.
**Send** wrong part numbers to store manager and check later corrections.
**Keep** crew site checks while new targets are tested.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour cuts, willing to test a useful tool.
S1.quote: A faster AI bracket order does not shorten the isolation check beside a live power line.
fieldNote: He **adopts** a new screen only on paid time with real repair sheets.
His **hours** worry comes from potential callout cuts, not a claim that robots have arrived.

steps.text: Learn AI ordering screen on paid shift with six repair sheets
Keep physical crew site checks while ordering targets tested

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could make plans when I am sixty, while capable line robots around 2031 could handle the pole when I am sixty-three. I would want the crew to stop a machine when the site does not match its plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot taking routine callouts could cut my pay before our retirement income is ready. Several months of savings and some nearby line jobs give options, but I cannot treat either as a guarantee of a full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request a written trial safety rule and a retirement income estimate. In the first year after 2028 I would compare any lost callout pay with that estimate, and I would look at written nearby lead vacancies only if the loss lasts two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about what could happen to paid hours, but not without a route to check. I need a real wage figure before changing jobs or stopping work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would trigger the crew to stop a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot may know the power line plan and still stand at the wrong pole tag. I would stop the machine at a wrong tag or isolation boundary. I would make the crew record the mismatch before any restart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a nearby lead vacancy need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Written pay at least covering our usual household costs and a reasonable journey. I would keep my current shifts until an offer was firm.

say: **Thinking** AI may plan by 2028; capable robots could reach poles around 2031.
**Crews** need authority to stop unsafe robot work.
think: **Routine** callouts could shrink before retirement income is adequate.
**Several** months saved and some local jobs give options, not wage certainty.
do: **Request** written crew stop rule and retirement income estimate this year.
**Compare** any lost callout pay with retirement costs after 2028.
**Check** nearby written lead vacancies if pay falls for two months.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss, with figures and local options to examine.
S2.quote: A robot may know the power line plan and still stand at the wrong pole tag.
fieldNote: He **wants** a stopping rule, but does not claim a certain job loss.
A **job** search starts only after sustained pay loss and depends on written offers.

steps.text: Check written nearby lead vacancies if callout pay falls for two months
Keep current repair shifts until a suitable written offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that thinking AI by 2031 reaches dispatch when I am sixty-three, and capable robots around 2034 reach field repairs when I am sixty-six. Five years is enough to test what a paid field verifier job actually entails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could supervise a robot repair check with my diploma and crew experience, but I do not know what income we will need at sixty-six. A title on its own will not cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the verifier course outline, pay and posted role details this year. If the company funds a hands-on course and posts a local verifier opening at no lower wage, I would enroll before 2031 and apply after the role opens; otherwise I would stay with the repair crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost field income, but there is time to compare real terms. I will learn a new checking duty once it is a paid job with work at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the hands-on course include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a damaged crossarm, a wrong pole number and a stop control in the same exercise. A line robot verifier should catch the wrong pole number before signing the machine’s repair safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the verifier opening is not local?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the travel and written wage with our household costs before applying. Some line jobs are nearby, so I would not move on an unposted promise.

say: The **longer** runway permits testing a paid field verifier role before robots arrive around 2034.
I would **require** physical fault exercises and worker stop controls.
think: My **diploma** and lead work might transfer, but retirement income remains uncertain.
A **verifier** job must offer real local work and at least current pay.
do: **Request** verifier course, wage and role details this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if hands-on course funded and local matching-pay role posted.
**Apply** after role opens if wage is no lower than current pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost income, with time to compare real offers.
S3.quote: A line robot verifier should catch the wrong pole number before signing the machine’s repair safe.
fieldNote: His **conditional** training requires company funding and a posted local role.
He **treats** the income estimate and actual pay as decision inputs, not a retirement promise.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if funded course and local matching-pay verifier role posted
Apply for posted local verifier role if pay matches current wage
Keep repair crew shifts if suitable paid role is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2036 comes when I am sixty-eight, and capable robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. If retirement income permits, I may have left the climb before either date; the apprentices still need sound physical checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have one to six months saved now, not a lifetime of income. I would like to stop full-time line work before seventy if the figures allow, but I cannot choose the exact year today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep normal shifts and ask for an updated retirement income estimate each year. If the amount covers our household costs before 2036, I would finish full-time line work then; if it does not, I would seek a posted paid ground-check role instead of assuming I can keep climbing indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the distant technology, careful about retirement arithmetic. A power line robot arriving at seventy-one may miss my climbing years, if our retirement figures actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a ground-check role include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would inspect completed repair sheets, pole tags and materials on site while another worker handles the climb. I would need written duties and adequate pay before taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach apprentices after leaving the climb?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would do paid practical days if offered, but I would not count that money in the retirement plan now. The company would have to put real hours on the rota.

say: A **decade** may place capable robots after my full-time line work ends.
**Apprentices** still need physical checks at poles.
think: **Several** months saved do not guarantee long retirement income.
I **may** stop full-time before seventy if actual income covers the household.
do: **Keep** normal shifts and update retirement estimate annually.
**Finish** full-time line work before 2036 if retirement income covers costs.
**Seek** posted paid ground-check role if retirement income stays short.
feel: **Calm** about late robots, careful with income figures.
S4.quote: A power line robot arriving at seventy-one may miss my climbing years, if our retirement figures actually work.
fieldNote: His **possible** exit is conditional on household income and should be counted as leaving the job.
The **fallback** ground job requires a posted paid role rather than a guaranteed offer.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and update retirement estimate annually
Leave full-time line job before 2036 if retirement income covers household costs
Seek posted paid ground-check role if retirement income stays short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach repairs at sixty-three before our retirement income is ready. Written crew stop authority, clear callout figures and paid field roles would help. I would rather keep a line crew working safely than race a robot to an unknown retirement number.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the young workers still get to read a broken crossarm at the pole. A training film will not give them the judgment a real fault gives. If a machine does the climb, the company still needs to pay people to check its work.

headlineQuote: I would rather keep a line crew working safely than race a robot to an unknown retirement number.
portrait: **Karl** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and careful habits around parts and isolation.
**Typical** pay, one to six months saved and some nearby lineworker jobs support him and his partner as retirement approaches.
He **uses** AI occasionally, tests new ordering on paid time and compares work changes with real field records.
He **considers** funded field verification or a conditional retirement exit only after written pay and household income figures are known.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031 while his retirement income and future callout pay remain uncertain.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** crew stop authority, clear callout records and real paid field roles would help him choose.
